summary: Reports a working system at Xerox in Palo Alto for sending text display information between a DEC PDP-10 running TENEX and a remote IMLAC PDS-1 display. It covers the IMLAC hardware, the facilities the user sees and the monitor calls on the TENEX side.

plainLanguage.summary: This report describes a system connecting a PDP-10 running TENEX to a remote IMLAC display. The main computer sends display commands, and the IMLAC shows text and returns user input.

subtitle: An operational system for sending display text between TENEX and a remote IMLAC.

tldr.problem: The report describes how a main-site computer can provide text display facilities to a remote graphics processor.
tldr.mechanism: A TENEX monitor on a PDP-10 sends command messages to an IMLAC, which displays text and reports keyboard or pointing-device input.
tldr.outcome: The system supports positioned display strings and a teletype simulation mode, with the PDP-10 checking identifiers and commands.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 190 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The text describes an operational display system in July 1971.

sections.title: The Two-Machine System
sections.content:
The report describes an operational system for sending textual display information between a main-site DEC PDP-10 running TENEX and a remote IMLAC PDS-1. The IMLAC is a 16-bit minicomputer with a display, keyboard and asynchronous serial interface.

The IMLAC can use an input interrupt feature, and the report recommends the SRI-ARC mouse and keyset, though the software can run without special hardware.
sections.plainLanguage: A PDP-10 runs the programs, while a separate IMLAC handles the display. They exchange commands and input over a serial connection.

sections.title: Display Areas and Modes
sections.content:
A console can show positioned text strings in display mode or show the latest 20 to 30 lines in teletype simulation mode. Programs can switch modes without losing information. A cursor string follows the pointing device.

In display mode, users receive rectangular display areas. A program can set each string's position, character size, font and horizontal increment independently, and manipulate one string without changing the others.
sections.plainLanguage: The screen can show text at chosen positions or act like a scrolling text terminal. It can divide the display into areas and update one string without changing the rest.

sections.title: Monitor Calls and Messages
sections.content:
TENEX programs use monitor calls to assign and remove display areas, write or move strings, set a cursor, and suppress or restore displays. Messages are sequences of 8-bit characters, with 7 bits carrying useful information and the high-order bit used for even parity.

Commands begin with an escape character and a count of following characters. Messages from TENEX carry display commands; messages from the IMLAC carry keyboard or other input. In long input mode, input messages can also include mouse coordinates.
sections.plainLanguage: The main computer sends short commands that tell the display what to show. The IMLAC sends back typed characters or input details such as mouse coordinates.

sections.title: Division of Responsibility
sections.content:
The PDP-10 allocates and checks display area identifiers and string numbers, so the IMLAC does not need to reply to every command. In the implementation described, display areas are numbered system-wide and strings are numbered within each area.

The PDP-10 cannot detect transmission parity errors or IMLAC memory overflow. The report says a secondary design goal was to keep display commands short.
sections.plainLanguage: The PDP-10 checks whether display identifiers are valid, while the IMLAC draws the result. Some transmission and memory errors remain outside the PDP-10's checks.
